Intrusive is darker in color; extrusive is lighter
questions.why_correct: Slow cooling underground allows time for large crystals to grow (granite). Rapid surface cooling doesn't allow crystal growth (basalt).
why_wrong: Intrusive is underground (plutonic); extrusive is volcanic — these definitions are reversed.
Color depends on mineral composition, not cooling rate.
The cooling rate difference produces significantly different textures.
questions.tip: Slow cool underground = big crystals (granite). Fast cool at surface = tiny/no crystals (basalt).

questions.q: How does sedimentary rock form?
questions.correct: Sediment is compacted and cemented together over time
incorrect: Existing rock is changed by heat and pressure
questions.why_correct: Weathering produces sediment; erosion transports it; deposition layers it; then compaction and cementation lithify it into sedimentary rock.
why_wrong: Magma cooling forms igneous rock.
Heat and pressure changing rock forms metamorphic rock.
Minerals crystallizing from seawater forms chemical sedimentary rock — a subtype, not the general process.
questions.tip: Sediment → compaction + cementation → sedimentary rock. Think: sand dunes → sandstone.

questions.q: Which rock type commonly contains fossils?
questions.correct: Sedimentary
questions.why_correct: Fossils are preserved in sedimentary layers because organisms are buried by sediment and preserved during lithification.
why_wrong: Igneous rock forms from molten material — no organisms can be preserved in it.
Metamorphic rock is altered by heat and pressure that would destroy fossils.
Neither igneous nor metamorphic rock typically preserves fossils.
questions.tip: Fossils = sedimentary rock only. Formed in layers where organisms are buried.

questions.q: How does metamorphic rock form?
questions.correct: Existing rock is changed by intense heat, pressure, or fluids (without melting)
questions.why_correct: Metamorphic rocks form when pre-existing rocks are subjected to conditions that recrystallize minerals — but the rock remains solid throughout.
why_wrong: Compacted sediment forms sedimentary rock.
Magma cooling underground forms intrusive igneous rock.
Dissolved and re-deposited rock forms chemical sedimentary rock.
questions.tip: Metamorphic = changed. Heat + pressure = mineral realignment. Shale → slate → schist → gneiss.

questions.q: What is the rock cycle?
questions.correct: The continuous process by which rocks are formed, broken down, and reformed over time
incorrect: The daily weathering of rock surfaces
The pattern of rock layers in sediment
questions.why_correct: The rock cycle shows how igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks can all transform into each other through geological processes.
why_wrong: Daily weathering is just one step, not the entire cycle.
Rock layers are stratigraphy — part of sedimentary geology, not the whole rock cycle.
Mineral classification is separate from the rock cycle.
questions.tip: Rock cycle = rocks constantly changing from one type to another over millions of years.

questions.q: What is the difference between a rock and a mineral?
questions.correct: A mineral is a naturally occurring solid element or compound; a rock is made of one or more minerals
incorrect: Minerals are man-made; rocks are natural
A rock is a single pure element; a mineral is a mixture
questions.why_correct: Minerals have a specific chemical composition and crystal structure. Rocks are aggregates of minerals (or sometimes organic material).
why_wrong: Size is not the distinguishing factor — minerals can be large, rocks can be small.
Minerals are natural, not man-made.
Minerals are pure compounds; rocks are mixtures of minerals.
questions.tip: Mineral = one specific chemical. Rock = combination of minerals.

questions.q: Which property is NOT used to identify a mineral?
questions.correct: Age
questions.why_correct: Minerals are identified by physical properties like hardness, luster, streak, cleavage, color, and density — not age.
why_wrong: Hardness (Mohs scale) is a primary identification property.
Luster (how light reflects) is a key identification property.
Streak (color of the powder) is often more reliable than surface color.
questions.tip: Mineral ID: hardness, luster, streak, cleavage, color, density. Age doesn't apply.

questions.q: What does the Mohs hardness scale measure?
questions.correct: A mineral's resistance to being scratched
incorrect: How much light a mineral reflects
The color of a mineral's powder
questions.why_correct: The Mohs scale ranks minerals from 1 (talc, softest) to 10 (diamond, hardest) based on which minerals can scratch each other.
why_wrong: Density is measured separately.
How light reflects is luster.
Powder color is streak.
questions.tip: Mohs scale = scratch resistance. Talc = 1 (softest). Diamond = 10 (hardest).

questions.q: What is luster?
questions.correct: The way a mineral's surface reflects light
incorrect: The color of a mineral's powder
The tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes
questions.why_correct: Luster describes the quality of light reflection — metallic (shiny like metal) or nonmetallic (waxy, glassy, dull, silky).
why_wrong: Powder color is streak.
Scratch resistance is hardness.
Breaking along flat planes is cleavage.
questions.tip: Luster = shiny or dull? Metallic (like pyrite) or nonmetallic (like quartz).

questions.q: What is cleavage in minerals?
questions.correct: The tendency of a mineral to break along smooth, flat planes
incorrect: The color of the mineral's surface
The pattern of crystals in the mineral
questions.why_correct: Cleavage reflects the internal atomic structure — atoms separate along planes of weakness, producing flat, smooth surfaces.
why_wrong: Surface color is just color — a less reliable property.
Hardness is the resistance to scratching.
Crystal pattern is the mineral's habit or crystal system.
questions.tip: Cleavage = flat, smooth break. No cleavage = fracture (rough, irregular break).

questions.q: Which mineral is the hardest on the Mohs scale?
questions.correct: Diamond
questions.why_correct: Diamond ranks 10 on the Mohs scale — it is the hardest naturally occurring substance.
why_wrong: Quartz ranks 7.
Feldspar ranks 6.
Corundum ranks 9 — second hardest, but diamond is hardest.
questions.tip: Mohs 10 = diamond. Mohs 1 = talc. Remember: TGCFAODQTC (Talc→Diamond).

questions.q: Which of these is a characteristic of ALL minerals?
questions.correct: Naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, with a definite chemical composition
incorrect: Always found in crystals you can see with the naked eye
questions.why_correct: All minerals share five defining characteristics: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, definite chemical composition, and crystalline structure.
why_wrong: Many minerals are nonmetallic and dull.
Many minerals have microscopic or invisible crystals.
Many minerals contain no silicon — for example, calcite (CaCO₃) and halite (NaCl).
questions.tip: 5 mineral traits: natural, inorganic, solid, definite chemistry, crystalline. All 5 required.
